ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: several days of feeling sick with a lower abdominal ache and a feverish sensation (hot and sweaty).
- Symptoms (onset/duration/severity/aggravating factors): onset about 2 days ago, duration ~2–3 days, constant dull ache in the lower abdomen, nausea but no vomiting, feverish with hot/sweaty feelings; increased urinary frequency without pain or urgency; constipation last week but currently resolved; pink/red tint in urine reported; no discharge.
- Past medical history: allergic to amoxicillin; uses Implanon (implant contraception); brother with type 1 diabetes in family; otherwise no other PMH noted.
- Medications/allergies: no current meds reported; allergy to amoxicillin.
- Family/social history: lives with boyfriend; non-smoker; sexually active; regular partner; implants in place for contraception.
- Vital signs/exam findings: not provided in transcript; patient described as feeling hot and sweaty; clinician noted need for examination; no specific vitals or exam findings documented in the text.
- Labs/imaging (if mentioned): none mentioned; doctor suggested pregnancy test and further examination/investigations.
- Additional contextual details: last menstrual period about 3 weeks ago; occasional spotting described as pink in urine; period due to around now; contraception is Implanon; no urinary pain or dysuria reported; no vaginal discharge.

V: Ovarian torsion or hemorrhagic/functional ovarian cyst with pelvic vascular involvement — rationale: lower abdominal ache that could reflect adnexal pathology with vascular implications; acute/subacute pain is plausible in ovarian conditions.
I: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — rationale: fever with lower abdominal pain in a sexually active patient; risk factors present (new or multiple partners implied by conversation); pelvic pain can be variable in PID.

Urinary tract infection / pyelonephritis — rationale: marked urinary frequency reported; feverish sensation; lower abdominal discomfort; UTIs can present with fever and suprapubic/abdominal pain even without dysuria.
N: Benign ovarian cysts (e.g., corpus luteum cyst) or other functional ovarian cysts — rationale: timing ~mid-luteal phase after LMP (~3 weeks ago); dull, constant pelvic ache; occasional light spotting can accompany luteal phase changes.
D: Constipation-related abdominal discomfort — rationale: history of constipation about a week ago; current pain could be multifactorial with intermittent stool-related pressure.
Dehydration-related symptoms or metabolic slowdown secondary to fever/nausea — rationale: feverish feeling and reduced intake could contribute to GI discomfort.
I2: Implanon (contraceptive implant) related side effects — rationale: device in place; known to cause irregular menses and abdominal/groin cramps in some patients; could contribute to pelvic discomfort.
Medication-related adverse effects (none currently reported) — rationale: absence of ongoing meds makes this less likely, but implant-related symptoms remain a consideration.
C: Early pregnancy complications (threatened abortion or ectopic pregnancy) — rationale: sexual activity with uncertain pregnancy status; last menstrual period ~3 weeks ago; pink-tinged urine could reflect early bleeding; pregnancy cannot be ruled out without testing.
A: Autoimmune/inflammatory mimics (less likely) — rationale: fever and abdominal pain could be from inflammatory processes, but autoimmune etiologies are less supported by current history without systemic signs or other organ involvement.
T: Acute appendicitis or other acute abdominal pathology — rationale: lower abdominal pain; fever could be present; location and character less typical for appendix but remains a differential until ruled out.
E: Pregnancy-related endocrine/metabolic states (early pregnancy) — rationale: pregnancy is an endocrine/metabolic condition; symptoms could reflect early gestational changes if pregnancy is present.
